newsitem.title: UK: UK M4 fall unlikely to end pressure for rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK M4 fall unlikely to end pressure for rate rise.

text.p: An unexpected fall in UK broad money supply growth in December was heavily distorted by repo transactions and will do nothing to stifle calls from the Bank of England for a rise in interest rates, economists said.

"At least M4 growth is back closer to the monitoring range, but I'm not sure if it will provide any great comfort to the market or the Chancellor in terms of an assessment of monetary conditions," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd.
The Bank of England said M4 growth fell by 0.2 percent in December, the first monthly fall since 1992.
Annual growth in M4 fell sharply to 9.6 percent from November's 10.8 percent.
Much of the deceleration was due to a drop in reverse repos included in M4 lending data, which the Bank attributed to a run-down of gilt repo activity over the calendar year-end.
But even stripping out these distortions, broad money growth was weaker than expected.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr said the distortions accounted for around 0.7 percent of the deceleration in M4, leaving an underlying annual growth rate of 10.3 percent.
"But even 9.6 percent M4 growth is still very strong and ...is inconsistent with the government's 2.5 percent inflation target as the Bank indicated last night," he said.
In an unusually forthright speech overnight in Edinburgh, George called for a pre-emptive rise in interest rates, adding that sterling's strength should not be used as an excuse to delay.
"George's comments overnight are a clear statement of his point of view and one month's distorted broad money figures are not going to change that view," said Shepperd.
George said: "There could be real dangers in allowing justified concern about the exchange rate to deflect us for too long from moving gradually to moderate the upswing."

Economists said Tuesday's quarterly trends survey from the CBI reinforced George's case for a rate rise."The most interesting point is what firms are looking to do with prices over the next four months," said Bank America's Jeremy Hawkins.

The survey showed the balance of businesses expecting prices to increase over the next four months rose to a positive 16 percent in January, from plus seven percent in October and minus one percent in July.

"Clearly the introduction of a new pricing list tends to bias up the prices side, but it does suggest there are some underlying concerns regarding cost pressures which are not appearing in the official statistics at the moment," said Hawkins.
"This is probably going to be leapt on by George as further proof of the need for some pre-emptive strike with regard to higher base rates."
Further data from the Bank of England showed M4 bank and building society lending fell by 3.8 billion sterling in December.
But the most robust area of bank lending -- to the personal sector -- remained strong, with a modest decline in lending for house purchase more than offset by a rise in other consumer loans.
"I don't think this changes the picture of strong personal sector credit growth," said Shepperd.
"The view that the consumer sector will still be strong over the next year and will drive the economy and generate above trend growth is unchanged."
